bio.en: Nancy Duarte is the CEO of Duarte Inc., which has created over 250,000 presentations for leaders including Apple, Google, and Al Gore, and author of books on the art of communication.
bio.zh: 南希·杜阿尔特（Nancy Duarte）是 Duarte 公司的 CEO，该公司为 Apple、Google、阿尔·戈尔等领导者创作了超过 25 万份演示文稿，她也著有关于沟通艺术的书籍。

summary.en: Nancy teaches the "contrast" framework - using the gap between what is and what could be - as a tool for influence in any format, from big stages to quick asks. She shares how even getting chores done at home can use persuasive structure. The episode is a tactical guide to presenting and communicating with impact.
summary.zh: 南希传授"对比"框架——利用"现状"与"可能"之间的落差——把它作为任何场合（从大型演讲到随口请求）施加影响的工具。她分享了即便在家让丈夫做家务，也能用说服结构。本期是一份关于"有影响力地演示与沟通"的战术指南。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: A lot of people think that the only time you really need to present well is when you have a big stage talk and you make the big investment in the script. The big investment in the contrasting story. I'll tell you a dirty little secret. I can get my husband to do chores for me on the weekends with a real quick, what is, what could be new bliss. So, the ability to just have that contrast as a framework in your brain during a meeting, on a phone call, any moment of influence, like literally it works. It works in any format.
turns.zh: 很多人认为，只有在进行大型演讲、投入大量精力准备演讲稿，或是讲一个反差鲜明的故事时，才需要好好展示自我。让我告诉你一个小秘密：我能让丈夫在周末帮我做家务，这简直是人生新乐趣。关键在于，在开会、打电话、任何需要施加影响的时刻，你能在脑海中构建出这种鲜明对比的框架——这真的很管用。无论何种场合，都能奏效。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Thank you for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many presentations have you helped craft at this point, both directly and indirectly?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，你们直接或间接地协助创作了多少份演示文稿？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: That's a great question. People know I'll like take a swag at data and pretend it's real. So, I had a president who took us a whack at that number in, it was 2014, and he said at that time it was 225,000, and that was almost 10 years ago, so I can't even tell you, I mean we stopped tracking, but it's a lot. I mean, in 35 years we have thousands of projects we open and each sometimes has two to a hundred presentations in it, so it'd be hard to tell.
turns.zh: 好问题啊，大家都知道我喜欢拿数据开玩笑，还把假数据当真。所以，有位总裁在2014年提过这个数字，当时他说有22.5万人——那差不多是十年前的事了，所以我也记不清了。毕竟我们后来就没再统计了。不过这个数字肯定很大。35年来我们做了上千个项目，每个项目有两到一百场演示，真要统计起来可太难了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: He said 250,000, but that was 10 years ago and I didn't do the math. So, when my team questioned it, I'm like, oh, Dan did the math. They're like, "Oh, then it's accurate." Because they thought I was just making up this number. I'm like, no, no, we actually went in and looked.
turns.zh: 他说的是25万，但那是十年前的事了，我当时没算过。所以团队质疑时，我说"哦，丹算过了。"他们回应"那数字肯定准了。"以为我在编数据。我说"不不，我们查过的。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I was not expecting it to be that large. That's insane.
turns.zh: 好吧。我真没想到数字这么大。太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It's so funny because I have the whole history of the Silicon Valley in a way. It's like every little startup and then they grew to massive brands like Cisco and you could actually look at the rise and fall of all these companies. And then I actually have all the decks. I still have a lot of these archives, so I could actually verify that number exactly.
turns.zh: 特别有意思的是，我对硅谷的历史了如指掌。看着每个小创业公司成长为思科这样的巨头，一路见证这些公司的兴衰起落。所有演示文稿我都保存着，现在还有大量档案，可以精准核实这些数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, well this next question's going to be extra hard then. Of all the presentations you've worked on, which one stands out to you as the most memorable or most impactful?
turns.zh: 好，那下个问题就更难了。在你参与过的所有演示中，哪一个最令你难忘或影响最深？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I mean, it has to be Al Gore's Inconvenient Truth. It kind of hit the world in a season where nobody really knew or had an example of a really well done presentation. So, it came out before TED Talks were even out on the web, and so people had never seen someone tell a data story and stand in front of data and the scale in 90 foot screen, but we had worked with him for five years before an Inconvenient Truth. People think he went from vice president to this presenter and I didn't work with him. I let my team work with him. So, they were the ones jetting around jumping backstage at Oprah. They loved it. It was a real peak season. (00:05:40): But the thing actually that was most memorable is we work with these 20 some year old CEOs here in the Valley and they tend to show up and act like they know better than someone who's been doing this for so long. And what was so interesting about this large figure politician communicator is the team would sit in a room and say, "Hey, we think you need to do this way. We think you needed to convey it this way. We think it should be visualized this way." Or whatever it was we were proposing. And he would literally pause and touch his chin and really think, and really consider that we might actually be experts. (00:06:18): And more times than not he would adopt the way we said it should be done. And so I think as the customer who actually probably had some of the most power in the whole world to thoughtfully defer to us as experts was delightful customer and consulting experience. I mean, I remember when they called me to say it was going to become a movie and that it had gotten funded and I started to get the information. They wanted us to do a lot of work to get it movie ready. And I'll never forget, I said, "Wow, that's going to be a lot of work we'd have to do for free, and who's going to go see a movie about a slideshow anyway?" That's literally what I said. So, yeah, I just didn't believe it would become what it became. So, the whole process was amazing.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，《难以忽视的真相》这部影片确实产生了巨大影响。在那个时候，全球还没有人真正了解或见过精心制作的演示文稿。影片上映时，TED演讲视频尚未在网上普及，人们从未见过有人在90英尺大屏幕前用数据讲述故事、与数据互动。但在《难以忽视的真相》问世前五年，我们就已经与阿尔·戈尔合作过了。人们总以为他从副总统一跃成为演说家，但实际上并非如此。我没有直接与他合作，而是让我的团队负责。正是他们频繁往返奥普拉的后台，兴致勃勃地参与其中。这确实是演示文稿行业的黄金时期。

（00:05:40）但最难忘的经历是，我们与硅谷那些20多岁的CEO合作。他们往往自视高明，认为自己比从业多年的老手更懂行。但这位政治传播巨星的团队会围坐一圈，说：“我们觉得你应该这样做。应该用这种方式传达信息。应该用这种视觉呈现方式。”无论我们提出什么建议，他都会停下来沉思，认真考虑我们的专业意见。多数情况下，他都会采纳我们的建议。我认为，作为客户，阿尔·戈尔这种愿意虚心听取专业意见的态度，是最令人欣喜的合作体验。

（00:06:18）记得当他们打电话告知影片即将开拍并获得资金时，我们接到大量后期制作任务。我永远忘不了当时的自己：“哇，这工作量可太大了，而且谁会去看一部关于幻灯片演示的电影啊？”这就是我的真实想法。是的，我根本不相信它会成就今天的规模。

整个过程堪称奇迹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you expect the impact of what happened after that presentation or was it just like, oh, we got this one job we got to do, let's just get through it and then move on?
turns.zh: 你当时预料到这场演示之后会产生如此大的影响吗？还是说你们只是觉得，哦，又接到一个任务，完成就行，然后继续下一个项目？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Well, we've been doing it for five years. I think the strategy, whether it was intentional or not, I don't know. So, he would go city to city to city, because he was traveling for five years seeding, like planting seeds for a groundswell, and he went into, he would go to the Stanford campus invite the Bay Area Elite, and it was always private and it was always VIP. And so he did a really good job for five years, traveling, traveling, traveling, traveling and really delivering that talk. And I think that created a desire. I don't know that it would've gotten that much traction. I don't know if people already didn't know about the presentation and hadn't already seen the presentation and they brought their friends to the movie, is how I kind of picture at least that part happening. (00:07:59): And he was generous, Lenny. I mean, at the end, when he traveled around for those five years at the end, he always had a slide with our name on it and would thank us if you're in the audience. I mean, super, and paid, mostly paid for what we did that we did give a lot of our own time. But yeah, super generous and yeah, movie became what it was. It was a bit of a surprise. It was good. The movie was good.
turns.zh:
嗯，我们为此准备了五年。我觉得策略是否刻意，我也不确定。但他会辗转各个城市，五年来不断播撒种子，引发公众关注。他会去斯坦福校园，邀请湾区精英，活动始终私密且邀请制。五年来，他在旅途中反复打磨演讲内容，最终成就了这部影片。我认为这份执着激发了人们的兴趣。我不确定它是否能获得如此广泛关注，但人们可能早就听说过这场演讲，也看过原版影片，甚至带朋友去电影院观看——至少这是我对当时情况的理解。
（00:07:59）阿尔·戈尔非常慷慨，伦尼。我记得在五年巡演结束时，他总会在幻灯片上写上我们的名字，并在观众席上致谢。真的太棒了，而且大部分费用都是我们自己掏的。但他的确非常大方，最终影片大获成功，着实令人惊喜。整体效果非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was good. It also makes me think about a pattern that I often see of it wasn't just one presentation that changed everything. It was, you said five years of prep ahead of that, and you always see these wow overnight success stories and you always find, okay, it wasn't actually that.
turns.zh: 挺不错的。这也让我想到一个常见的现象——并非只有一次演讲就能改变一切。正如你所说，这背后往往有五年的准备工作。人们常看到那些一夜成名的惊人故事，但最终发现其实并非那么简单。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, and he did a good job after, once it got traction, we built a whole training program where he could fly people out to his place in Tennessee and start to train people. So, it almost became a train the trainer and he could sanction you as a ambassador for it. So, it was just the way the whole thing kind of unfolded and scaled and then got traction was lovely.
turns.zh: 是啊，在它获得关注后，他做得很出色。我们建立了一个完整的培训项目，让他能把学员们带到田纳西州的基地进行培训。这几乎形成了一个“培训师培训”的模式，学员们通过他的认证就能成为该项目的大使。整个事情的发展、扩展和推广过程都非常精彩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of impressive clients, I only learned this recently, but Apple has been a client of yours since the day you were founded as an organization. Is that right?
turns.zh: 说到令人印象深刻的客户，我最近才知道，苹果从你们组织成立之初就一直是客户。对吗？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, it was. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. How did you land that initially? And then also just what have you learned from that experience that's informed your approach to presentation, design, communication, and how you work with clients?
turns.zh: 好的。最初你们是如何拿下这个客户的？从这次经历中，你学到了哪些东西，影响了你后续在演示、设计、沟通以及与客户合作方面的方法？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I love that question. So, yeah, I had a real job. I was working my real job and my husband had bought a Mac and he's like, "I think this is a business. I think it could be a real business." And he was an illustrator, wasn't a designer, but he had been a fine artist. And he's like, "Look, I can draw." Of course it's all pixelated and bit mappy. He goes, "Look, I could draw lines in here." And if I could show you his art studio, his work is just gorgeous. So, he's definitely a fine artist. And he's like, "I think this is a business. I think this could be a business." And I'm very pregnant. We were talking about that earlier. I am very pregnant with my son and I'm like, "Dude, you're going to go get yourself a real job. I don't want you playing around with this little Mac thing." (00:10:02): And he begged me twice in our marriage. He literally has gotten on his knees and to try to get me to see his perspective begged me. He's like, "Just read a Mac World magazine, just read it through once, and if you still don't think this could become a thing ..." Because I was working on a mainframe, I'm like, I work on a real computer. So, what happened was I made some phone calls. I called NASA and I called Tandem, which is now HP, and I called Apple and we won contracts at all three brands at the same time. And back then our company was called Duarte Desktop Publishing and Graphic Design.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这个问题。是的，我当时有一份真正的工作。正在做我的本职工作，我丈夫买了一台Mac电脑，他说：“我觉得这能成一门生意。真的能成为一门生意。”他原本是插画师，不是设计师，但曾是优秀的艺术家。他说：“看，我能在这儿画线条。”当然，画面全是像素化和有锯齿的。他又说：“看，我能在这儿画线条。”如果能让你看看他的艺术工作室，他的作品简直美极了。所以他绝对是个优秀的艺术家。他接着说：“我觉得这能成一门生意。我觉得这能做成一门生意。”而我当时怀孕了，我们之前提到过。我怀着儿子，怀孕已有数月。我说：“老兄，你得去找份正经工作。我可不想你玩这些Mac小玩意儿。”（00:10:02）他在我们的婚姻生活中求了我两次。他真的跪下来求我，让我听听他的观点。他说：“你就看看《Mac World》杂志，通读一遍，如果你还是觉得这玩意儿没前途……”因为我当时在大型主机上工作，觉得自己用的是真正的电脑。结果我打了几个电话，分别联系了NASA、Tandem（现为惠普）和苹果，结果同时拿下了这三个品牌的合同。当时我们的公司叫Duarte桌面出版与平面设计公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I know, I know. And we slipped in. When you talk about a product lifecycle, very early, everything was still bit mappy, was not attractive. Most people as users didn't know how to typeset, didn't know how to do columns, didn't know how to make in this tool at all. And there's about an 18 month window in the life cycle of the Macintosh where graphic designers refused to use it, refused. It's a toy, it's ugly, it's bit mapped. Nobody would do it, a font like that. We use Linotype. It was very, the snobby kind of, we won't touch it. And that's right when we entered right then went and checked out books at the library on type setting, we tried to figure out what we could do, what could we do with this tool, and then the rest was kind of history. And so that's how it started and the timing and just kind of pushing the tool that nobody was that interested in that we're in the design community. It was small adoption.
turns.zh: 我知道，我知道。我们就这么悄悄钻了进来。当你谈到产品生命周期时，早期阶段一切都还很不成熟、毫无吸引力。大多数用户当时根本不懂得如何排版、如何设计栏目、更别提如何在这种工具中操作了。在Macintosh的生命周期中，约有18个月的时间，平面设计师们都拒绝使用它，坚决抵制。他们认为它就是个玩具，外观丑陋，采用位图技术。当时大家都用Linotype字体，业内人士曾不屑一顾，断然拒绝尝试。我们却在那时悄悄行动起来，去图书馆借阅排版相关的书籍，研究如何利用这款工具发挥创意。接下来的事就顺理成章了。整个过程始于机缘巧合，抓住了设计界对这款鲜为人知工具的兴趣空白期。最初用户接受度极低。

turns.en: So, that's interesting that it was cold emails basically are cold reach out just like, "Hey, we want to work with you." Yeah, that's an awesome [inaudible 00:11:42]-

turns.en: What did you take away from that experience that kind of informed what works and doesn't work in presentations?
turns.zh: 从那次经历中，你获得了哪些启发，哪些经验能指导你如今的演示技巧？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Presentations used to be 35 millimeter slides in an old carousel. In fact, that's what Al Gore had when he showed, he was like, here's my slide carousel from the seventies. It was just how it was done. But Apple was the first company to hook up the computer to a projector at scale. Now the projectors at these big venues like San Jose Convention Center, I mean it was huge and it was risky. So, because we were first in, they pushed us to start to do the presentations in this tool and it was black and white. Everything was black and white when we first started. And then we started to push and push and push from how we illustrated things in the tool, how we would colorize clip art. I mean, I'm talking like clip art packages just came out and they're like, "Hey, grab these, colorize them." (00:12:32): And so it was a really momentous moment to win them as an account. And I remember the tool had started to really take off and it was ugly. You can call it fugly, I don't know what you want to call it, but everyone who made slides did it so poorly, just so poorly. And we were kind of pushing the boundaries of it to make it look attractive. And there was a sales conference in 1992 in San Francisco and the leader of sales at the time was kind of a creative savant of sorts. And I remember he's like, "I don't know how you're going to do it, but I want you to take the whole slide." This is when slides were basically teleprompted covered in text. If you could stick a piece of clip art on it, you were lucky. And he said, "I want you to just make the whole slide, it's just covered with the word big in hot pink. And I want the background black, because when this slide pops up in all pink big, I want it to actually light the faces of the people in the audience." (00:13:26): And it was like I didn't know how to, we couldn't do that. We had to go into free hand, convert it to this, do these six steps, and then we came up with a small JPEG at the time or png or something and we scaled it up. So, it was still kind of pixelated. And I remember I was in that hall during the rehearsal and the production team gasped. Couple people squealed. They're like, "Who did this? I mean, it was just the word big in magenta pink." And I just remember thinking, this is how it's supposed to be done. Putting the tool in the hands of the masses kind of destroyed the medium itself. (00:13:58): And I feel like the first 10 or so years I was in business, it was reshaping this medium that ran amuck when it got into the hands of the users, it just went completely the opposite way that it was supposed to. So, it's weird to say that was a real defining moment for me to say, wait, we can do this different and we can return to how they used to be done when they were 35 millimeter slides. So, that's one story. And then I think we're very good at mapping to the brand requirements. So, we take this tool, whatever the tool, we have all our brands use different ones. They use Slides, Keynote, they use PowerPoint. We use whatever tool the brand wants and we push it in each medium. But we take their brand guidelines and really push it into the spoken word medium where when they stand up on a stage, it's cinematic. The visuals can become an experience in itself. (00:14:57): And I remember when Apple came up with the Think Different campaign. Steve Jobs was just back and my designer, everyone Photoshop was new. And everyone's doing these beveled backgrounds with tons of crap on the background. And I walked by, I'm like, "No, oh, we can't have a blue frame looking photo frame to for the Think Different campaign. This is not going to work." And so I remember looking at all the posters and remembering the Alfred Hitchcock ones. It had these particulates like these particulates, and it was just shadows. (00:15:34): And I found a stock video that Adobe had made at the time, and it was just particulates floating through the air at the angle and we stuck the six color apple on top of it. That was so revolutionary back there to push the brand and get out of the way every, the whole world was making these hideous templates. So, there are these moments that pushed the company forward because of an idea that I knew would not be okay for the Apple brand, therefore it shouldn't be okay for any brand. And I think those are just a couple stories of how to really push the medium in a way that is more pleasing to the audience. The audience just likes it better when it's really clear what you're supposed to focus on. We love that brand. We love it.

过去的演示文稿都是35毫米胶片幻灯片。事实上，阿尔·戈尔（Al Gore）在展示时用的就是这种设备，他说自己用的是70年代的幻灯片播放器。当时就是这么操作的。但苹果公司是首家大规模将电脑与投影仪相连接的公司。如今，在圣何塞会议中心这样的大型场馆里，投影仪规模巨大，且风险颇高。因此，作为先行者，苹果公司迫使我们开始使用这款工具进行演示——当时一切都是黑白的。我们刚起步时，所有演示文稿都是黑白的。随后我们不断突破技术界限，优化图像效果，比如给剪贴画上色。（00:12:32）  
签下这个客户堪称重大突破。当时这款工具刚起步，界面丑陋不堪。你可以称它“难看至极”，我不知道该怎么形容。但所有制作幻灯片的人都做得很糟糕。我们不断突破界限，让界面更具吸引力。1992年在旧金山举办的销售会议上，当时的销售主管堪称创意天才。我记得他说：“我不知道你们怎么做到的，但我要你们把整个幻灯片都用粉色大字覆盖。”那时的幻灯片基本是照着提词器制作的，能加个剪贴画就算幸运了。他要求：“把整个幻灯片都用粉色大字覆盖，背景设为黑色。当粉色大字突然跳出时，要照亮观众席上的面孔。”（00:13:26）  
当时我们完全不知道该怎么做，只能手动操作，转换格式，完成六个步骤，最后生成当时的小型JPEG或PNG图片，再放大。但图像还是很模糊。排练时，我在大厅里，制作团队惊呼几声，有人尖叫：“谁做的这个？就一个大大的粉色字母！”我记得当时想，这才是正确的操作方式。将这款工具交到大众手中，反而毁了整个媒介。（00:13:58）  
在入行的前十年，我致力于重塑这个被用户滥用的媒介，最终走向相反的方向。于是我意识到，回归35毫米胶片时代的演示文稿才是正确的方向。这就是一个故事。  
此外，我们擅长根据品牌需求定制工具。无论是Slides、Keynote还是PowerPoint，我们都会让品牌使用适合他们的工具，并在各个平台推广。但我们会严格遵循品牌指南，将设计理念融入口语化表达，让演讲者在舞台上呈现出电影般的效果，视觉效果本身就能成为一种体验。（00:14:57）  
记得苹果推出“非同凡想”（Think Different）广告时，史蒂夫·乔布斯刚回归，设计师们对Photoshop还很陌生。大家都在用带有大量装饰的斜边背景。我路过时说：不行，我们不能用蓝色边框当相框来展示“非同凡想”。
不同的宣传活动。这招根本行不通。” 于是我记得自己当时看着那些海报，脑海中浮现出阿尔弗雷德·希区柯克的电影海报。那些海报只有一些细微的颗粒感，全是阴影。（00:15:34）后来我找到了Adobe当时制作的一个库存视频，画面中各种细微的颗粒在空中飘浮，角度恰到好处。我们把六色苹果标志放在画面上方。在当时，这简直是个革命性的创意，既能提升品牌形象，又能避开当时全球普遍使用的那些难看模板。正是这样的创意时刻，推动了公司向前发展——因为我深知，这样的创意若用在苹果品牌上肯定不合适，所以它也就不该用于任何品牌。我觉得这只是几个成功案例，告诉我们如何真正突破媒介界限，创造出更令观众满意的作品。当观众能清晰明白你希望他们关注的焦点时，他们会更喜欢这样的设计。我们热爱这个品牌，我们深爱它。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Your audience is the hero. That was in my TED talk from 2011. I would say it's infuse your talk with story. And I would say it is asking yourself, can they see what I'm saying? Those would be the three tips other than starting with empathy. I mean that that's, well, audience is the hero, is the empathy centric approach.
turns.zh: 听众是主角。这是我2011年TED演讲中的核心观点。我建议在演讲中注入故事元素，并时刻自问：他们能理解我要表达的意思吗？除了从共情入手，这三个要点还包括：听众是主角，以及以共情为核心的演讲方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's dive into these then. And I was actually going to ask around empathy, and it feels like that comes up a lot in your recommendations to people's empathy is kind of the heart of your methodology of telling great stories, telling great presentations. So, let's spend a little time there. Why is that so important and what does that actually look like in practice?
turns.zh: 接下来我们深入探讨这些要点。你提到的共情在你的建议中反复出现，似乎是讲述精彩故事、做好演示的核心方法。能否请你详细讲讲，为何共情如此重要？在实践中又该如何具体操作？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Empathy is important to Duarte, everything we do is empathy first. And some of it comes from my own childhood story a little bit. I was raised by a clinically narcissistic mom and narcissist are missing the empathy gene. So, I feel like that void of not having it modeled for me is why I keep clawing at empathy as being important. And I think a lot of people listening might work for a boss that does not have empathy, that isn't other centric, that doesn't think before they talk and all of those things. And I was raised by someone like that. And so every single book and every single model that I ever make has empathy at the core because you have to have to think about who am I speaking with, especially in communication, who am I speaking with? And so when I went on my journey through storytelling, I figured out that I thought, okay, the presenter's the hero, for sure the presenter's the hero, they're the central figure. They're talking the most. They're well lit, they're up on a stage. (00:18:48): So, when I started to look at all the archetypes, that's where I landed. And then I was like, oh my god. When I got to really digging into the mentor, I realized it's really the mentor in myths and movies that's the presenter and who really holds the power in the room of a presentation is the audience, the audience gets to make a choice if they accept or reject your idea. So, the balance of power is with them and not you. So, it really is the role of the presenter to be the mentor. And in myths and movies, the mentor comes alongside the hero. In other words, the presenter should come alongside the audience and help them get unstuck or bring a magical tool. So, I think Obi Won Kenobi's a great example. (00:19:32): He did two things for Luke Skywalker. He gave him a light saber, which was for his outer journey, the physical journey he was doing, and then an inner tool, which was the resolve, which came to him through the force. So, when you're speaking to an audience, they're going to have an internal conflict that you have to give them something to soothe. And then you're asking them to therefore go and do this thing, take this action, do this call to action. That's asking them to physically do something or physically change in some way. So, they're not going to do that for you if you haven't empathetically thought about how hard what you're asking them is going to be for them to do. And so you have to change your mindset when you're starting to build your deck to think about who am I talking to? How am I going to help them get unstuck? And that's just a super foundational principle in everything we do.

杜阿尔特认为同理心至关重要，我们所做的一切都应以同理心为先。这在一定程度上源于他童年时期的经历——他由一位临床自恋型母亲抚养长大，而自恋者恰恰缺乏同理心基因。因此，他深知自己童年缺乏同理心模范的成长经历，这正是他始终强调同理心重要性的根源。他相信，许多听众可能正为缺乏同理心的上司工作——那些以自我为中心、说话前不经思考的人。而他恰恰由这样的人抚养长大。

因此，他创作的每一本书、设计的每一个模型都以同理心为核心。正如他所说：“你必须思考与谁对话”，尤其是在沟通场景中，要始终以听众为中心。通过研究叙事理论，他发现传统演讲者常被视为英雄中心人物，占据舞台焦点，但观众才是真正的权力主体——他们有权选择接受或拒绝你的观点。

这启发他将演讲者的角色转变为导师：在神话与电影中，导师与英雄并肩同行；演讲者应与听众建立联结，帮助他们突破思维障碍，或提供神奇的解决方案。例如，《星球大战》中的欧比旺·肯诺比为卢克·天行者提供光剑（外在助力）和原力赋予的内在决心（精神指引），后者才是真正改变听众的关键。

当面对听众时，演讲者必须化解他们的内心矛盾，提供切实可行的行动指南。若未能感同身受，听众将难以践行你的建议。因此，设计演示文稿时必须始终以听众为中心，思考如何帮助他们克服障碍。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Oh, that we know about. So, I could talk about our own internal ones. Most of what we do is under MSAs because they're fantastical brands. So, in my own company, before I do a presentation that's going to require goals or them reaching goals or we do an annual vision talk, we do a listening tour first. So, some of it's based in survey, some of it's based in interviews. And we feed that information up and then we compare it to what we're going to ask them to do. And we do some gap analysis. We literally, there's some actual questions you can ask yourself, which are somewhat classic design thinking kind of questions about where they're at. And then what we do is I create a real rough cut or the exec team creates a real rough cut and then we invite the next level of leaders in and we do a fake, I mean the slides are ugly, we don't spend time on the slides. (00:21:31): This is about the message and maybe a model or two or three that we're going to go through to feel like it may amplify or make the message more concrete. And then they get feedback and that's when it's hard. It's hard to go from rough cut, here's what we're going to say to making it absolutely resonate. And then we deliver it after all of that work has been done, then we share it to the company. So, we go through that knowing that's the hardest presentation I deliver all year. I used to travel and speak and be a public speaker, but it's my own internal ones I have to take more time with. (00:22:05): So, when I travel and speak, they're like, oh my God, I love your models. Oh my gosh, can I get a picture with you? But when I'm standing in front of my own team, they're like, I wonder what she's going to say, because she's about to either make my job harder or she's going to change my priorities. They come in more skeptical. And we definitely have nailed the annual kickoff meeting. Definitely have nailed that. And then we do quarterly updates to that annual kickoff meeting. And it's a cadence and people get enthused and we're kind of killing it right now.
turns.zh: 哦，这方面我们很清楚。所以，我可以谈谈我们公司内部的情况。我们大部分工作都是在MSA框架下进行的，因为这些品牌太出色了。在我的公司里，每当要做需要设定目标、让团队达成目标的演示，或者召开年度愿景会议时，我们都会先进行倾听之旅。有些信息基于调查，有些基于访谈。我们收集这些信息后，再将其与我们要求员工达成的目标进行对照，并进行差距分析。我们会提出一些经典的设计思维问题，比如了解他们的现状。然后，我们会制作一个初稿——虽然幻灯片很简陋，但我们不会在这上面花太多时间。（00:21:31）：这主要传达信息，可能还需要一两个模型来加深理解。之后，他们会给出反馈，而这正是最困难的环节。要从初稿过渡到真正能引发共鸣的演示，需要耗费大量心血。完成所有准备工作后，我们再向全公司发布。这场演示是我全年最难完成的任务。我过去常到处演讲，但现在我更专注于内部演示。（00:22:05）：当我外出演讲时，人们会说：天啊，我喜欢你的模型。哦，天哪，能和你合影吗？但面对自己的团队时，他们会说：她要说什么呢？她是要让我的工作更难做，还是要调整我的优先事项？他们更加持怀疑态度。不过我们确实把年度启动会议做得很成功。确实如此。之后我们每季度会对年度启动会议进行更新。这种节奏让人们兴奋不已，目前我们做得非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to walk through these three bullet points. So, the first is make the listener the hero of your story. And that comes from being empathetic and understanding their challenge. Or what should people identify of I'm doing this well or I'm not doing this well?
turns.zh: 我想讲讲这三个要点。第一个是让听众成为故事的主角。这需要同理心，理解他们的挑战。那么，如果你想做到这一点，有哪些迹象能表明你做得好或者不好的呢？比如故事的开场方式是怎样的？是那种“事情是这样开始的”吗？或者人们应该如何判断我做得好还是不好？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: If the audience is the hero, you would see visible signs that they get it. People would come before I did a really good talk and people were tweeting saying, "Hey, come to this talk. It's really good." So, you'd see a reaction. You know you've done it well if you're infusing your talk with story, which is the second bullet by utilizing story structures. So, when I say storytelling, I'm talking about an anecdote. When I say story structures, I'm talking about this format of a three act structure of storytelling that goes back tens of thousands of years, which is fused into the brain like FMRI machines now you can see them while a story's being told and the science is beautiful, if you're telling me a story and I'm listening, our brains are firing in the exact same order, in the exact same place. So, it has power to align our brains. (00:24:26): And so by implementing attributes of story like a beginning, a middle, and an end, and we have method for that. And in also incorporating the rise and fall story kind of builds tension and releases it. And that's why we love it so much is we escape through someone else's messy middle and conflict and problems like it's messy and then it resolves. You build the tension and resolve it. And that's what a really well structured presentation can do. It can pull on that rise and fall in a way that creates longing. (00:24:58): So, story creates longing. It helps people long for something they'd never wanted before because if the future is told in the shape of a story and they see this alternate future, so many people escape through sci-fi. They escape through movie making into these future worlds. And so picture that you could verbally paint a picture of this future state and then you could bring your whole audience to this future state in an amazing way using this cadence of rise and fall. That's how you can incorporate story into a presentation where you need to influence others, actually really can be beautiful when it's done well.
turns.zh: 假如听众是主角，你会看到他们明显的理解信号。比如，在我做了一场精彩演讲之前，就会有人主动前来，并在推特上写道："嘿，快来听这场演讲吧，真的很棒！" 所以你能感受到他们的反馈。如果你能在演讲中融入故事元素（这是第二个要点），利用故事结构来传达信息，那你就知道自己做得很成功了。我所说的讲故事，指的是分享趣闻。而我所说的故事结构，则是指数万年前就形成的三幕式叙事模式。如今，功能性磁共振成像（fMRI）技术已经证明，当人们聆听故事时，大脑会以完全相同的顺序、在完全相同的区域产生反应，这种科学现象非常神奇。比如，当我给你讲故事时，你在听的过程中大脑活动的顺序和区域都完全一致。这足以说明故事能调动我们大脑的共鸣。（00:24:26）通过运用故事的基本要素——开端、发展和结局，我们就能掌握其中的方法。同时，融入起伏交错的叙事结构能制造紧张感并释放压力。正因如此，我们如此热爱这种叙事方式——通过别人的混乱历程、冲突与困境，我们得以逃离现实，体验另一种可能。先制造紧张感，再化解矛盾。这正是精心构思的演讲所能做到的，它能巧妙地利用起伏结构激发人们的渴望。（00:24:58）故事能激发人们的渴望。它能让人们对从未渴望过的事物产生向往。比如，科幻作品中的未来世界，电影构建的未来世界，人们都沉浸其中。想象一下，如果你能用语言描绘出这种未来图景，再通过起伏的叙事节奏将听众带入未来场景，这将是多么美妙的体验。当你需要影响他人时，将故事融入演讲中，效果会非常惊艳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so you gave a TEDx Talk on this exact topic. And so I want to go deeper here. And you kind of shared this very visual way of thinking about a great story where it kind of goes up and down and up and down these teeth almost. Can you actually talk about-
turns.zh: 所以你曾就这个主题做过TEDx演讲。接下来我想深入探讨一下。你分享了一种用视觉思维构建精彩故事的方式，故事的起伏就像齿轮般交替。能否具体谈谈——

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: [inaudible 00:25:51] pumpkin teeth. Yeah, it does.
turns.zh: [00:25:51不可听清]南瓜牙。是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you share what that structure visually looks like? And we'll share a link in the show notes of what that actually looks like and then just why that is so impactful and important.
turns.zh: 能否分享一下这种结构在视觉上的呈现方式？我们会在节目笔记中附上相关链接，展示具体效果，以及其背后的影响力和重要性。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, I love that. So, I went on a three year journey through story and I knew that the greatest speeches overall time did have that rise and fall and rise and fall. But it wasn't one single story. It had a whole lot of other very important information, but it still did this rise and fall and risen fall. So, I am not a digital native. I took a quarter inch graph paper and I would listen to all kinds and map out, took the words. When I analyzed Steve Jobs's iPhone launch speech, I did it all by hand. I wrote every word I did quarter inch graph paper. I needed to know, I needed to see it the way I work, which was analog. And so at first it was zigzaggy and I realized, wait, you can't map something over time and have it be a zigzag. (00:26:49): There was too much data lost. So, to verbally describe it, you could picture a line at the bottom of your screen and that line going left to is what is. And you need to set up every talk by stating what is. And then it moves straight up and you move to what could be come back down to the bottom line again say what is, back up, what could be, what is, what could be, what is, what could be? And then at the last what could be you state the last horizontal line is what we call the new bliss. So, this motion of traversing between what is, what could be, what's is, what could be, what is, what could be, that sense of longing for the future, it makes people leave their current state or the status quo or our current reality and makes them long for this future state by using contrast. (00:27:37): So, that rise and fall of hey, here's our current problem, here's a solution, or here's the state of the union. But we imagine it could look like this. There's so many different ways to build that cadence of contrast that's so lovely. I mean it really works. I think the talk came out in 2011 and the amounts of notes and emails of things people have accomplished by changing the structure of their presentation has been really astounding.
turns.zh:
是的，我特别喜欢这种方法。所以，我花了三年时间研究演讲技巧。我发现历来最伟大的演讲都遵循着起起落落、再起起落落的结构。但这绝非单一的故事——它们还包含大量其他重要信息，然而整体节奏始终是起落交替。（0分26秒）我不是数字原住民。我用四分之一英寸的方格纸手写笔记，分析史蒂夫·乔布斯的iPhone发布演讲时，每个字都是用笔写出来的。我需要用手写的方式来理解演讲的结构，符合我的工作习惯——即模拟思维方式。最初的结构很混乱，我意识到，时间线上的起落交替无法直观呈现。（0分27秒）用口语化的方式来描述，你可以想象屏幕底部有一条线，从左到右延伸，代表现状。每场演讲都需要从现状出发，逐步构建可能的未来状态，再回到现状，如此循环往复。最后再用最后的可能性来勾勒出我们所称的“新福音”。这种在现状、可能性、现状、可能性之间来回切换的节奏感，让人们渴望突破现状、迎接未来，通过对比产生张力。

（0分28秒）所以，这种起落交替的结构——比如“这是我们当前面临的问题，这是解决方案”，或者“这是国家现状”——但我们设想它可以这样：有很多方法能构建这种对比的节奏感，它真的很有效。我记得2011年发布那次演讲后，无数人通过改变演讲结构取得了成功，收到的反馈令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The State of the Union is a really interesting example because I'm trying to imagine this and presentations I've seen and that totally resonates of just like, here's the problem we're having and here's where we're going to go. Here's another problem we're having. Here's what I'm going to change.
turns.zh: “国情咨文”是个非常有趣的例子。我试着想象这种结构，回想我见过的演讲，它们都遵循着同样的模式：这是我们当前面临的问题，这是我们要去的方向。再来一个问题，这是我要改变的。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Steve Jobs was great at that. When he launched the iPhone speech, he always did, here's the state of the company, here's how we're doing. Oh my God, our stores are more full than 10 Mac world expos. He always did a setup of what was going on. And then he did a really rapid what is, what could be when he started to compare the iPhone to the Blackberry. It's like, look how much it sucks now that you've seen what we're doing. It's just what is, what could be, what is, what could be. And so I took all the classic speeches, historical speeches, everything, presidential speeches and knew that if I could find a pattern in Dr. King and Steve Jobs's iPhone launch speech that was the same, that had the same type of nature of cadence and pulsing to it, for lack of a better word, that I knew I had solved it using story. It was a really great moment to finally draw that out on my quarter inch graph paper.
turns.zh:
史蒂夫·乔布斯在这方面堪称典范。他发布iPhone演讲时，总是先讲公司现状，再讲进展。天哪，我们的门店比10次Mac World展会加起来还要火爆。他总会先铺垫现状，再在对比iPhone和黑莓时快速呈现“什么是可能”和“什么是现状”。这就是“现状、可能性、现状、可能性”的节奏感。

我研究了所有经典演讲、历史演讲、总统演讲，发现如果能在马丁·路德·金和乔布斯的iPhone发布演讲中找到相同的模式，具有相同的节奏和脉动感（找不到更合适的词汇），我就知道我用故事结构成功了。最终在四分之一英寸的方格纸上画出这种节奏感，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这种方法了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It was awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like there's just so much opportunity for primary research that still I feel like that's why my newsletter does well is I just spent the time doing that work that you're describing of watching a thousand interviews and then just distilling, here's a takeaway here.
turns.zh: 我觉得有很多机会可以进行原始研究，但我觉得这也是我的新闻通讯能做得好的原因——我花了大量时间做你所描述的工作，观看上千个采访，然后提炼出关键要点。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Pattern finding, that's an interesting point. I worry sometimes with the emergence of new technologies and stuff, the ability to be able to sit and think, synthesize and all of that is because a human's going to come up with different insights and synthesis than any future machine can do. So, I think it's fascinating that you do that so well and it really shows that.
turns.zh: 模式识别，这是一个很有趣的观点。有时我会担心，随着新技术的兴起，我们静下心来思考、综合信息的能力可能会退化。但人类总能提出比任何未来机器更具洞察力和综合性的见解，所以你能把这件事做得如此出色，真的很了不起，这也充分证明了这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I appreciate that.
turns.zh: 哇，太感谢了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, you're really putting your mind and heart into it all.
turns.zh: 是啊，你真是全身心投入其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Enough about me, I'm thinking about, but I appreciate it, I'm thinking about product managers and founders maybe listening to this and they're like, oh man, every time I do a deck, I need to create this whole story and this up and down thing. In your experience, when do you go that far to create? Is this when you have an epic important presentation, you think about a story structure like this, or is there always a way you should put this into your presentations of some kind of story with this contrast?
turns.zh: 说到我自己，我一直在思考，但我很感激听到这些话。我在想，或许正在听节目的产品经理和创始人会说：天啊，每次我做演示文稿时，都需要构思整个故事线和起伏情节。以你的经验来看，你会在什么时候下如此大功夫去构思？是面对重大演示时，才会考虑这种故事结构和对比手法吗？还是说在任何演示中都应该融入某种对比鲜明的故事？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It's interesting question. I think a lot of people think that the only time you really need to present well is when you have a big stage talk and you make the big investment in the script, the big investment in the contrasting story. But I'll tell you a dirty little secret. I can get my husband to do chores for me on the weekends with a real quick, what is, what could be new bliss, kind of just that first bit, what is, what could be new bliss. It's like even the very, very short talk that Abraham Lincoln gave in the Gettysburg address, it was basically a funeral, it was a eulogy. And back then eulogies used to be two hours long. It was an Aristotelian structure and he only had a couple hundred words, so there's no pictures of him giving it because it was so short, so tight and done. (00:31:16): They were setting up the cameras, still thinking they had tons of time. So, the ability to just have that contrast as a framework in your brain during a meeting, on a phone call, any moment of influence, getting the husband to do some chores for me, literally it works. It works in any format. And I think the investment that you make in the longer form or when it's a huge audience, you add the visuals, you really hire the speaker coaches, you really make that moment. And there's these moments that breach above all other moments where you really have to nail it just in basic conversations, in a moment of influence. If you practice it enough, it'll live in your head as a mental model for when you're in a situation where there's influence in the air that you could do.
turns.zh: 这是个很有趣的问题。我觉得很多人认为只有在大型演讲、投入大量精力写脚本、设计对比鲜明的故事时，才需要好好准备。但我要告诉你一个小秘密。我能很快让丈夫帮我做周末家务，用“什么是，什么可能是新的幸福”这种简单开场，引发对方兴趣。就连亚伯拉罕·林肯在葛底斯堡演讲的简短发言，也不过是场葬礼致辞，当时致辞通常长达两小时。这是亚里士多德式的结构，而他只有几百字，所以没有他的演讲画面，因为内容太简洁、太紧凑了。（00:31:16）当时摄影师还在架设备，以为时间充裕。所以，在会议、电话或任何施加影响的时刻，能在脑海中构建这种对比框架真的很有效。甚至能让丈夫帮我做家务，这在任何形式下都管用。我认为在长篇演讲或面对大量听众时，再加上视觉效果、聘请专业演讲教练，才能真正打造出震撼人心的时刻。但有些时刻比其他时刻更重要——那些在基本对话中、施加影响的关键时刻。如果你反复练习，它就会深深印在你的脑海中，成为应对各种影响时刻的思维模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you actually do it with your husband if you could share for helping you do the dishes?
turns.zh: 你能分享一下如何让丈夫帮你洗碗吗？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Well, I won't get graphic about what the new bliss might be, but early in our marriage we figured out that, not early, I actually spent almost in the only the last 10 years we've been married for 40. And we realized that when we tangle it's usually only about process. So, the gaps are if I ask or he asks me to do something or we start to kind of pick on each other, it's because the way I'm executing something is different than the way he chose to execute it. And so it'll be anything from like, "Why are you chopping onions like that?" He'll say to me. And now I'm like, oh, we have a process gap. "Do you want to chop the onions or do you want me to chop them my way?" So, for the what is, what could be new bliss, it happens all the time. (00:32:59): So, he needs a lot of context. He's a detail-oriented person and I've started to learn with him that my what is needs to be quite a bit longer than sometimes I have patience for as I start to frame, "Oh hey baby, I need you to take the dog over to the dog care." I don't start there. I start with, "Oh my gosh, tomorrow I've got back to back meetings, in fact, I'm going to be on Lenny's Podcast right about here. And that's when she's whiny. And what's going to happen is if that doesn't happen, I'm going to have to reschedule next week and next week it's just loaded up. And you know how it is when I'm stressed out at the end of the day and I'm kind of hard to deal with and I say, well, what could be, the doggy place, she was loved it last time she was spooning with a red cavalier king spaniel and loved it." (00:33:46): It's like that, I have to unpack it a little bit more for him. And then the new bliss could be any sort of marital promise you want it to be, but I just have to unpack the current state a little bit of the process, and then I state what could be. And it's funny because acts of service like that, like him taking the dog to the doggy daycare for me or is I feel loved. So, when someone does something generous with their time for me, it's how I feel loved. And so there's a whole lot there in shaping how you communicate with someone. Empathetically at my company, everyone knows each other's love language. They know that this person feels more appreciated when they get a written note. This person feels more appreciated when they get a gift and everyone knows that. So, that's just baked into our, I don't know, our marriage, our company, just how it rolls.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不想详细描述新的“幸福”是什么，但在我们刚结婚时，我们意识到——不，准确来说，是我意识到——在过去40年的婚姻里，有将近10年我们都在处理“流程问题”。当我们产生矛盾时，通常只是因为我执行某件事的方式和他选择的执行方式不同。比如，他会问我：“你为什么要那样切洋葱？”然后我就会意识到，我们之间存在流程差异。“你是想自己切，还是让我按我的方式来？”所以，当我们谈论“现状”和“可能的新幸福”时，日常对话其实都是在探讨流程问题。（00:32:59）他需要详细的背景信息。他是个注重细节的人，我逐渐学会了为他提供更完整的信息。比如，当我说“亲爱的，你能带狗狗去狗狗日托所吗？”时，我不会直接切入主题，而是先说：“天哪，明天我有连场会议，事实上，我还要参加Lenny的播客节目。到时候她可能会闹脾气。如果不按计划进行，我就得重新安排下周的日程，而下周我的日程已经排满了。你知道的，一天结束时我压力大的时候，脾气会很差。”（00:33:46）这就是关键，我得为他把事情拆解得更细致。然后，新的“幸福”可以是任何你希望的婚姻承诺，但首先我得剖析现状，理清流程，再构想未来可能的样子。这很有趣，比如像他带狗狗去日托所这样的善举，就能让我感受到被爱。当有人为我付出时间时，我会感受到被爱。所以，沟通方式的塑造至关重要。在我的公司，每个人都知道彼此的爱的语言。有人觉得收到书面感谢更感激，有人更喜欢收到礼物，每个人都清楚这些偏好。所以，这已经融入了我们的婚姻和公司文化，自然而然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine people listening to this podcast were not expecting marriage advice. And so I love that. I'm going to try.
turns.zh: 我猜听这个播客的人都没期待婚姻建议。我喜欢这样。我要试试看。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: You can scrap that if it doesn't work the process tip though is good.
turns.zh: 如果不奏效，就把流程部分去掉，但流程小贴士还是不错的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is going to be the best part. This is going to be the whole podcast is just the segment. Just joking. But this is really good advice. I'm going to try to use it myself. So, the structure, I think it's even easier to think about this less as story, infused story. For me it's more this, what is, what could be, what is the ideal bliss, that's almost the simpler way to think about it. The story is this like, oh my God, I got to think of a story.
turns.zh: 这会是最精彩的部分。整个播客可能就围绕这个环节展开。开玩笑的。但这些建议真的很棒。我要试着自己应用。结构方面，我觉得不必把它想得太复杂，少些故事，多些逻辑。对我来说，更重要的是“现状”、“可能的新幸福”以及理想的幸福状态，这样更容易理解。故事部分就比如，“天哪，我得想个故事。”

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It has a beginning, middle, and an end. So, the first, what is is the beginning. The middle is the messy middle. That's where you're trying to contrast and show them that it's messy. It might be hard, it's worth it. And then the new bliss, you end with what in western cultures, where's like a happy ending. So, the new bliss is just imagine a world with your idea adopted, and then you paint a picture of that world poetically or pragmatically, and it works. It definitely works.
turns.zh: 它有开头、发展和结尾。所以，首先，什么是开头？发展阶段就是混乱的中间部分。在这里，你需要形成对比，让听众看到混乱的局面。这或许会很艰难，但最终是值得的。然后是新生欢乐的部分，在西方文化中，这部分通常代表着美满的结局。所以，新生欢乐就是设想你的理念被采纳后的世界，然后用诗意或务实的方式描绘出这个世界，这样做肯定行之有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is really great. So, just to recap, point one is to make your listener the hero of the story and come at it with empathy. And I was actually thinking the Think Different campaign is an excellent example of that because it's about you thinking differently and being this incredible creative. And then item two is infuse your presentation with story and this what is, what could be new bliss. And then, okay, and number three, what was number three again?
turns.zh: 好的，这真是太棒了。总结一下，第一点是让听众成为故事的主人公，并以同理心来传达你的观点。实际上，我觉得“Think Different”广告活动就是一个很好的例子，因为它鼓励人们以不同的视角思考，展现出非凡的创造力。第二点是用故事来充实你的演讲，比如现状和新生欢乐的部分。第三点，第三点是什么来着？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Oh, it was ask yourself if they can see what you're saying. Can they see what I'm saying would be written on the note?
turns.zh: 哦，是问自己听众能否理解你所说的内容。假如笔记上写着“他们能否理解我所说的内容”会怎样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. Okay, let's talk about that. What does that mean and how do you do that?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个观点了。好的，我们来深入探讨一下。这意味着什么，又该如何做到呢？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, so for people to see what you're saying, that you have an opportunity to use visual tools like the presentation software, you have opportunities to have live sketchers sketch it while you're talking. There's so many ways you can help people see what you're saying. I would contend that you can use something in your talk that gives people something they'll always remember. We call that a star moment. And it could be a piece of dramatic data where the big numbers put up there. It could be an evocative story, it could be a beautiful picture. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You were just talking about process and that is a great segue to a question I wanted to ask is just what does your process look like when you're working with a company to help them craft an awesome presentation?
turns.zh: 你刚刚谈到流程，我正好想问个问题，就是当你为公司打造精彩演示文稿时，他们的流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. It's funny because I don't have to do this much anymore. I haven't done it for about 15 years, which is nice. I have a gorgeous team of strategist, writers, conceptual thinkers, beautiful design.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。有趣的是，我现在不怎么做这事了。我已经有15年没做了，这倒挺好的。我有一支很棒的团队，里面有战略家、写作人员、概念设计师，还有出色的设计师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was curious.
turns.zh: 我很好奇。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Coaches. Yeah, I know. I get coached. It's fun. I definitely, my books look awesome, not because of me, but because I'm followed around by people that do really gorgeous work. But the phrase that we use internally and sometimes with customers is we make presentations the way Pixar makes movies. And that's very similar to the way we get somebody that has this high stakes moment where it's a big deal in this moment. You have to win in the moment to push things along. And so we do, we literally craft a narrative, craft the big idea, craft the script and visualize certain moments. We start to map it out, we start to chunk it out. (00:51:05): And then big models sometimes when you're really making a revolutionary model, one that could drive all the web assets, a lot of that stuff people don't realize actually happens in the presentation first as an idea. So, sometimes we'll start working on some of the key models right away too, and we start to circulate that around the company, because everyone has to build consensus around it. So, sometimes there's multiple motions happening at the same time. Let's sketch this. You go away, you work with this department, you try to get this settled, you get that set, you get this. (00:51:36): And then it gets reassembled at the end. And then the narrative is where you work all the kinks out and then when they stand and deliver, it's like, yes, it's the voice track that all the process supported. And then other times we're building a report in a slide doc, or there was a time where we had a head of a multinational company that will remain nameless and the guy that was head of all of India was going to come over here and petition the CEO for a hundred million dollar budget. (00:52:09): It's not trivial. And he comes, is like, "Okay, I need your help with these five slides." And he just sends us the five slides and we're like, "Well yeah, a hundred million. That's kind of a lot. You really want to put technology between you and the CEO. Do you really want to sit side by side and both be looking at a computer in this moment where it's like you're petitioning him for, that's a lot of money." And he's like, "Yeah, you're right." So, what we did is we made a mental model he could hold up in his head and the structure was so simple and clear. And then there was three moments where we're like just, I don't know, just grab a piece of paper or go to a whiteboard and just start to draw in front of him. Let him see your eyes, let him have eye contact. (00:52:46): Let him see your passion. Don't be dispassionately looking at this computer. And he did it and he called us and he's like, "I got a hundred million bucks." So, it's just those moments where you have to realize, wait, wait, wait, wait. Do I need a deck? Who am I talking to? And should is this a cookie cutter thing? And does the same process work every time? No. So, every time we solve something it's very different and we try to make it unique to the presenter and the audience that they're speaking to.
turns.zh: 教练。是的，我知道。我自己也接受过指导。这很有趣。我的书看起来很棒，不是因为我，而是因为身边有才华横溢的人在帮忙。但我们内部团队以及与客户合作时常用的说法是，我们制作演示文稿的方式就如同皮克斯制作电影一样。这和我们如何帮助那些面临重大挑战、事关重大的客户非常相似。你必须在当下赢得胜利，才能推动事情进展。因此，我们会精心构思叙事主线、提炼核心创意、撰写脚本并设想关键场景。我们先进行框架规划，再逐步细化。（00:51:05）有时当你正在打造革命性的模型——一个能驱动所有网络资产的模型时，这些创意往往最先以演示文稿的形式呈现。因此，我们有时会立即着手设计关键模型，并在公司内广泛征求意见，因为每个人都需要达成共识。有时，多个项目会同时推进。比如，我们会先构思草图，然后分发给各部门，让他们协同解决问题。（00:51:36）最后，再将所有元素整合成完整的演示文稿。通过不断打磨叙事逻辑，最终呈现出凝练有力的成果，而这份成果正是整个流程所支撑的核心理念。还有时候，我们需要制作幻灯片报告。曾有一位不便透露姓名的跨国公司高管，负责印度业务的总裁即将来此向CEO申请1亿美元预算。（00:52:09）这可不是小事。来访者说：“好的，我需要你帮我做这五张幻灯片。”他只发送了五张幻灯片，我们回应：“嗯，1亿美元啊，这可不小。你真的想用科技手段隔着屏幕向CEO汇报吗？你真的想和他面对面坐在电脑前请求拨款吗？这可是一大笔钱啊。”他点头说：“对，你说得对。”于是，我们为他构建了一个易于理解的思维模型，结构简洁明了。在三个关键节点，我们拿起纸笔或在白板上即兴作画，让他直视我们的眼睛，保持眼神交流，感受到我们的激情，而不是冷漠地盯着电脑。最终他成功了。他打电话告诉我们：“我拿到了1亿美元。”这就是那些需要停下脚步、审视自身的时刻：我需要幻灯片吗？我面对的是谁？这是一刀切的模板吗？每次方案都适用吗？不。所以每次我们解决问题时，都会因人而异，为演示者和听众量身打造独特的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, a lot of presentations now are actually remote and on Zoom and virtual. What do you recommend to people in terms of how they present and put presentations together being remote?
turns.zh: 同样，现在很多演示都是远程进行的，通过Zoom等平台进行。针对远程演示，您对人们有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny, we spent a lot of time coaching people to look in the camera. So, while I've been talking to you, I'm not actually looking at your face. I'm looking at the little dot at the top of my screen and my camera. And not a lot of people can do that. So, it's gotten to where I can see that little white glowing dot and my heart warms, I know you're there, I feel you. I can get sensations in my skin when I know I'm talking to someone that I adore or admire. And that took a long time to get there. And I was presenting remotely pre COVID. So, a lot of our coaching was about eye contact and doing that. The other thing that happens is people don't see our hands anymore. They're under the table. They can't see how much space in a room we're taking up. (00:54:15): They can't see a lot of the characteristics that are common in communicating. And so there's a lot of coaching around presence and how do you have presence in a room? How do you even get the microphone away from someone that's remote and all those kinds of things. And a new study just came out, I just came across my desk today and it said that soft skills really suffered. And the people who did it right say and looked at the camera, they don't have good eye contact skills anymore. When they are looking face-to-face in someone's eyes, it's like, oh, they're not used to it. It's been so long. (00:54:50): And then the other thing is, where do I sit in a room who's got the position of authority? Just kind of some classic things that convey information in real life. So, it's interesting, it peaked and now people are going back to the office some. A percent are back in the office. And now we have this weird place where it's, oh, it's half in the office and half people are remote. And the people that are remote are having a hard time getting their voices heard because the people in the room consume most of the air. So, it's kind of going through this undulating life cycle of new communication skills people need while they're remote. It's all changing.
turns.zh: 是啊，这挺有趣的。我们花了大量时间指导人们注视镜头。所以，当我和你们交流时，我其实并没有看你们的脸。我看的是屏幕顶部和摄像头上的那个小白点。但很多人做不到这一点。现在只要我能看到那个小白点，我的心里就暖暖的，我知道你们在听，我能感受到你们的存在。当我知道自己在和心仪或敬仰的人交谈时，皮肤都会产生触电般的感觉。要达到这种状态可不容易。新冠疫情之前我就已经在远程演示了。所以，我们当时的大部分指导都围绕眼神交流展开。另外，有些人看不到我们的手了。手都藏在桌子底下了。他们也看不到我们在房间里占据的空间。（00:54:15）他们看不到很多日常交流中常见的细节。因此，我们需要反复指导如何展现存在感，以及如何在房间里掌控局面。最近有一项新研究，我今天刚看到，研究称软技能确实受到了影响。那些正确注视镜头、保持眼神交流的人，现在已经不具备良好的眼神交流能力了。当他们面对面注视对方时，对方会说，哦，他们不习惯了。已经太久了。（00:54:50）还有一个问题是，在有权威地位的会议中，自己该坐在哪里？这些都是现实生活中传递信息的经典技巧。所以说，有趣的是，现在远程办公已经达到了顶峰，人们又开始部分返回办公室了。有百分之多少的人回到了办公室。现在我们处于一个奇怪的阶段，一半人在办公室，一半人远程办公。远程办公的人很难让自己的声音被听到，因为办公室里的人占据了大部分的氧气空间。所以，在远程办公时代，人们需要掌握的新沟通技能正经历着起起落落。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad that I was not a PM in this remote world to be honest. I never experienced it, but I have a lot of empathy for being a product manager in this remote work world. Feels like the job got a lot harder.
turns.zh: 说实话，我很庆幸自己在这个远程世界里不是产品经理。我从未经历过远程工作，但我对身处远程工作环境中的产品经理们深感同情。感觉这份工作变得难多了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It did. I think it did.
turns.zh: 确实如此。我觉得是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, let's talk about nerves and stage fright. So, I hate public speaking. I get extremely nervous people. They may not feel this when they watch me, but it's not my natural state. You work with a lot of people that I imagine are like, oh my god, I'm so scared to give this presentation. What advice do you give them to help them through that and feel more comfortable?
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，让我们来谈谈紧张情绪和怯场。说实话，我讨厌公开演讲。我会变得极度紧张。你们看我演讲时可能感觉不到，但这并非我的自然状态。你和很多人一起工作，我想他们会说，天哪，我好害怕做这个演示。你会给他们什么建议来帮助他们克服紧张情绪，感觉更自在呢？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, I think people who are more thoughtful and contemplative about speaking have better content. They tend to really think through stuff than someone who's like, I got this. I'll just wing it. I'll just walk on the stage. Anyone who's like, tells me I am a nervous presenter, I'm like, you have probably got gorgeous content in your heart that the world needs to hear, because usually they are really deep and thoughtful. Like you already mentioned, you're a pattern finder and you like to do thoughtful work. And so it's hard. My husband is actually a brilliant communicator, just getting him to feel like he wants to take up the space. He's a better communicator than I am. And so what happens is the reason you get scared, it's a fight or flight instinct. For some reason stepping out on that stage, you feel your body and your mind and your psyche is feeling threatened like you would be attacked by an animal. (00:56:56): That's literally what's happening. And so you couple things you could do. You can actually sit in one of the seats of the auditorium and just sit there and look at the stage, look at the setting so you can imagine yourself on it. But then picture yourself as that friendly face, the one that's happy to see you, the one that's delighted that you're speaking. And then as you're standing up, remember that you saw yourself sitting there smiling and very happy. You have to change your visual model that people's faces will be scowling, they'll be judging you, they'll be doubting you. All of those things are only in your head because getting you out on the stage to be able to start to expose people to this amazing content you have, the biggest battle is to get you out on this stage and delivering it. (00:57:47): And I asked a bunch of people once, I did a survey of all these public speakers and was like, how do you prepare? How do you prepare? What's your pre-talk ritual? And some of them were like, "I play heavy metal music and I skip around the entire convention center, just get all fired up." I'm like, "Wow, I have to calm myself down because I already have over to the top energy." So, I literally find the dark. I don't go to the green room, that stuff. I don't like to hear gibber jabber. I have to be focused on my content. And so I find the darkest corner of the backstage and calmly sit and just breathe. I just breathe. Sometimes if I'm nervous, if there's someone real famous in the audience, I have a little list playlist of funny things that people sent me, but I never watch. And that way right before I walk on stage, I chemically, my whole body chemically shifts from nervous to laughter. And that really helps me too, because it's chemical and you have to train your chemistry a bit.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得那些在说话时更深思熟虑、善于反思的人，总能创作出更优质的内容。他们往往会认真思考每个细节，而不像有些人那样觉得“反正我准备好了”，随意上台。那些被说成是“紧张型演讲者”的人，我会回应：“你心里可能藏着让世界聆听的精彩内容，因为他们通常都深思熟虑、富有洞察力。” 就像你提到的，你善于发现模式，喜欢进行深度思考。这确实不易。我的丈夫实际上是个出色的沟通者，但要让他觉得自己能掌控全场却很难。他比我更擅长表达。恐惧感源自“战斗或逃跑”本能。当你站在舞台上时，身体和心理会产生被攻击的威胁感。这就是大脑的真实反应。所以你可以尝试几个方法：先坐在观众席上，观察舞台环境，想象自己站在台上时洋溢的亲切笑容。上台前，要记得自己曾坐在那里面带微笑、神采飞扬。改变思维模式——别把观众想象成冷眼旁观的批评者，而是充满期待的朋友。  

另外，我曾调查过许多公众演讲者：如何准备？他们的预演仪式是什么？有些人说：“我听重金属音乐，在会场跳来跳去，激发热情。” 我则说：“哇，我得先冷静下来，因为我已经精力过剩了。” 我会刻意寻找安静角落，避免被外界干扰。观众席的休息室太吵了，我只想专注于内容。  

上台前，我会找最昏暗的后台角落，深呼吸放松。如果紧张时，台下有名人，我会播放别人发来的搞笑视频片段，瞬间将化学反应从紧张转为欢笑。这就是情绪管理的奥秘，需要刻意训练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that tip. What are these funny things you watch if you-
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个建议。要是你看这些搞笑视频——

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It's like YouTube things, TikTok things. Just things that I tag and I try not to watch them or things that make me laugh. There's this dorky low watched video of a guy with tin cans wrapped around his waist and he plays them. And my husband walks around the house like him and making the noise and I could probably sing the beat if I had to. And so sometimes I just play that, because it just transports me home, because a lot of times I'm presenting away from home and it just makes me laugh at my husband who's hysterical. So, it's just random things, but if you laugh and somehow can transport yourself outside of the fear of walking out there, it helps reset you before you walk out on stage.
turns.zh: 这就像YouTube上的视频、TikTok上的内容。就是我标记的那些视频，我尽量不去看，或者那些能让我开怀大笑的视频。比如有个视频，讲一个家伙用锡罐缠在腰间玩耍。我丈夫在家也模仿他的动作，发出那种声音。要是让我唱那个节奏，我肯定能唱出来。有些时候我就会播放那个视频，因为它能让我瞬间回到家乡的感觉，毕竟我经常在外地演讲，听到丈夫那滑稽的模仿声，总能让我忍俊不禁。所以说，这些都是些零零碎碎的小玩意儿，但只要能让你笑出来，暂时忘却走上舞台前的恐惧感，就能帮你调整好状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that. Is there anything else just off the top of your head that just like right before you go on stage that you find to be really effective? So, watching funny videos, I love that. [inaudible 00:59:47] use it. Anything else?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这样。还有没有什么突然想到的办法，能在上台前快速调整状态？比如看搞笑视频，我超爱这个。[0:59:47不可听清] 我现在还用这个方法。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I breathe. I think I've learned a breathing pattern. I take a deep, deep breath and then I take that one while my lungs are full, I take another gulp of breath and I have to let it out real slow. But when I got the feedback that my friend and some people get over their fear by headbanging to heavy metal, so I'm not saying that's not the wrong thing. So, I thought, well, maybe I should try that before I do a talk. And so I literally didn't do that. But I stretched, I jumped a little, just low jumps, put my arms real big up in the air. And then I walked on stage and I happened to be speaking at a massive medical company, like big brand. And I finished my talk and my assistant got a call and they were like, "We're little worried about Nancy. We think she might need to see a doctor. She could never control her breathing and we're really concerned." (01:00:38): And it was just because I just pumped myself up a little bit. So, I don't do that whatsoever anymore. I went back to my calming, contemplative, meditative pre-talk ritual. So, for some people, literally I do encourage people to try headbanging to heavy metal. It might work. It's just a matter of what you need. And nobody would guess that I'm not one to dance around or pump myself up, but I am not, I have to calm myself down. It's the opposite.
turns.zh: 我会深呼吸。我觉得自己掌握了一种呼吸技巧。先深深吸一口气，然后屏住呼吸，再深呼吸一次，最后慢慢呼出。但我听说有些朋友通过跟着重金属乐摇头晃脑来克服恐惧，我不觉得这招不对。所以我就想，或许我上台前也该试试。不过我最后没这么做。我只是做了些拉伸，跳了几下小幅度的跳跃，双臂高高扬向天空。结果我走上舞台时，正好是在一家大型医疗公司演讲，那个品牌如雷贯耳。演讲结束后，助手打电话来说，"我们有点担心南希，她控制不住呼吸，感觉很不舒服。"（01:00:38）结果只是因为我稍微给自己打了打气。现在我再也不用这种方法了。我又回到了平静、专注、冥想的演讲前准备流程。有些人我真的会鼓励他们试试摇头晃脑听重金属乐，或许会有用。关键在于找到适合自己的方法。没人能想到我不爱跳舞、兴奋过度，但事实并非如此，我需要冷静下来。恰恰相反。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Just a few more questions.
turns.zh: 太棒了。再问几个问题。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you wrote a book called Illuminate and something that stood out to me from that book is this idea of a torch bearer and torch bearer leader. Can you just talk about what that is and why that is important in power?
turns.zh: 你在书《Illuminate》中提到"火炬手"和"火炬手领袖"这个概念。能谈谈这两个概念吗？为什么它们在权力领域很重要？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, I loved writing that book. Co-author Patty Sanchez, a hat tip to her. So, to come up with this book, we knew that there's one presentation, there's a single presentation, could be on a stage, could be in a meeting, just updating people on a project status. And we knew though that every presentation usually is part of a larger movement where you're trying to move people in mass to this alternate future. So, we studied movements, we deconstructed the largest movements. We met with Marshall Ganz at Harvard to say, "Hey, could this be true?" Because he studies movements. It was so fun. And then movements have a five act structure. So, picture, there's this moment where you have to verbalize the dream like, hey, we're going to head to this new place and this is what I have to do at my kickoff meetings. It's like imagine this place in the future that we're headed to. (01:02:15): So, it's five steps, it's a five act story structure, if you want to call it five acts. It's dream, leap, fight, climb, arrive. So, the torch bearer, the reason we called that is the leaders know where they're headed, but they might not ever see it super, super clearly. And we chose a torch because a torch, if you're in a cave and you have a torch, you only see about five, eight feet around you, but it's enough to dissipate the fear of the people following you in. And so nobody sees the future clearly. Nobody has that kind of level skill. All we know is I need to traverse this direction to be at the right place in the future so all my staff is safe, all are, we stay a leader in the industry. That's all I know. And as we start to head there, there's these moments of communication you need to do, which is, hey everyone, here's the dream. Here's where we're headed. That's the dream phase. (01:03:09): Then there's this moment where they either choose to jump in and go with you or they choose not to. You could talk about Frodo like Sam and only a few hobbits followed him. And so it's like people select to commit this journey. That's the beginning of your movement. But then the middle is the messy middle of a story. We call it the fight and climb phase. So, what happens is they commit to your idea, they commit to your program, your project, and they're like enthused at first. And then they go into the state of, oh my God, this is harder than I thought. It's a long slog. This climb is getting exhausted. I don't know if I have this much fight in me to make this all work, not fight with each other, but like, oh my God, I'm having to overcome this roadblock and that roadblock and we have to go get that budget. (01:03:53): So, it's just, it's like a fight, climb, fight, climb, fight, climb. And then ultimately you arrive. Each one of those five phases you need to use speeches, stories, ceremonies and symbols at each phase to give the people traveling with you the emotional fuel they need to keep going, to keep seeing that idea become realized. And it literally is about fueling the right emotions with speeches, stories, ceremonies, and symbols while you're moving people toward a bigger initiative. So, it's bigger than just one presentation, it's multiple presentations, multiple stories, multiple ceremonies. So, I loved that book. People are really feeding off of it right now because leading change has been nonstop. It's just been change, change, change the last especially few years.
turns.zh:
是啊，我很喜欢写那本书。还要特别感谢我的合著者帕蒂·桑切斯。说到这本书的创作，我们深知每场演讲都是一个单独的展示，可能是在舞台上，也许是在会议上，向人们汇报项目进展。但我们也清楚，每场演讲通常都是更宏大行动的一部分——你试图带领人们走向一个全新的未来。因此，我们研究了各种运动，剖析了最成功的行动范例。我们还拜访了哈佛大学的马歇尔·甘兹，向他请教：“这真的可行吗？”毕竟他是研究社会运动的专家。这整个过程充满乐趣。运动往往遵循五幕结构：设想、跳跃、抗争、攀登、抵达。（01:02:15）  

我们将领袖比作火炬手，因为领袖们清楚目标方向，但未必能看清全貌。火炬象征着黑暗中的指引。正如洞穴中的火炬，光线仅能照亮五到八英尺范围，但足以驱散追随者的恐惧。未来本质上是未知的，没人能预知全貌。我们只需确保团队安全抵达目标，确保行业领导地位。  

在前行过程中，需要多次沟通：向团队传递愿景、召集同行参与。这是梦想阶段。（01:03:09）  

接下来，追随者要么选择加入，要么选择退出。正如《指环王》中的山姆与佛罗多，只有少数霍比特人追随英雄。这是运动的开端。中间阶段则充满挑战，我们称之为抗争与攀登阶段。团队最初满怀热情，投入项目，但随后会遭遇阻碍，比如预算申请受阻。这是情感波折阶段，需要用演讲、故事、仪式和象征符号为追随者注入燃料，帮助他们克服重重障碍。  

最终抵达目标。五个阶段中，每一步都需要用演讲、故事、仪式和象征来激发追随者的情感动力。整个过程就像抗争、攀登、抗争、攀登、抗争、攀登，最终抵达。  

我深爱这本书。如今人们对其借鉴频繁，因为领导变革的挑战从未停歇。过去几年间，变革的脚步从未停歇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Change is the only constant like they say.
turns.zh: 正如人们所说，变化是唯一不变的常量。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this metaphor of the torch giving you a sense of, as a leader, you can see some portion around you, but you're not going to see the entire cave necessarily. That is really interesting. Maybe a final question very tactically is I give an interview where you shared that you had kind of two videos, one where it's very informal, you're just standing in front of whiteboard in jeans or something, just talking about some about data, I think in presentations. And then you had a similar video where it was very well constructed, high production value, and the informal video did a lot better. Is that something you're seeing? Just that kind of content ends up being more successful and why do you think that is?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个比喻——手电筒能照亮你周围的部分，但不一定能照亮整个洞穴。这真的很有趣。最后一个很实际的问题是，我在一次采访中提到，你有两个视频版本，一个非常随意，你就站在白板前，穿着牛仔裤之类的，只是谈论一些数据，可能是在做演示。另一个视频制作精良，质量很高，但那个随意的视频效果要好得多。你有没有注意到这种情况？为什么这种内容更成功？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I think video content, production quality now isn't the expectation for it being high quality. It's just completely shifted over the last five, eight years or so as everyone's an expert and can show up as an expert. There's a big difference to me about showing up as a keynoter, which is like, I'm going to stand, I'm going to look right. I'm going to have this eye contact, I'm going to nail it. My slides are gorgeous, I'm driving the industry. And for people to think that our explanations of things needs to be done as a stand and deliver keynote, that's just not true. So, I experimented with that and I had some videos I had done, and one of them, like you said, was me looking in the camera. I even had HD makeup, a film crew. I was well lit, I looked amazing. I mean, I did look amazing and it was polished. (01:06:09): I delivered it really well. And then I thought, because on LinkedIn I post a lot, that's where my primary channel is, and I thought what would happen if I just posted a rando shot of me? And I'm maybe airing on a little bit like orange, I look a little Trumpian, a little bit orange. It's not color corrected, but it's super informative, really full of information. And that was my highest viewed video so far. And I realized that it's like people want the content and we do as a presentation company, I have to nail it maybe more than others, but it doesn't have to be fully video edited, infographics spinning, swooshing things forward and swooshing things back. (01:06:50): That kind of nature of it is not necessary to get the message across. And so we actually have a whole process and program we're rolling out where you're going to see a lot more video from us, partially from that insight, but partially because my team, I have a team of experts, they have a lot of great things to share, and so I'm trying to give them, I'm trying to make it be like Duarte does not equal Nancy Duarte. I'm trying to make it so it's like so many experts work at Duarte, you got to watch any video from any of them is where we're moving at Duarte. They're freaks of brilliance and just experts. They're world class experts. So, that's what we're trying to do.
turns.zh: 我认为视频内容的制作质量现在已经不是人们的期望了。在过去五到八年间，情况完全变了，因为现在每个人都是专家，都能表现得像专家。在我看来，作为主讲人出场的标准完全不同了。比如，我要站在台上，保持眼神交流，表现出专业形象。我的幻灯片要美观，引领行业潮流。但人们却认为我们的讲解内容必须像主讲人那样严谨，这完全不对。所以我尝试了这种方式，制作了一些视频。其中一个，正如你所说，是我对着镜头讲话的。我甚至化了高清妆容，请了摄制组，灯光很好，看起来很棒。（01:06:09）：我讲得很好。然后我想，在领英上我经常发帖，这是我的主要平台，如果我只是发一张随意的照片会怎样？照片里我可能有点偏橙色，看起来有点像特朗普，有点发黄。没有经过色彩校正，但信息量很大。这成了我迄今为止观看量最高的视频。我意识到，人们需要的是内容。我们作为演示公司，确实要比别人更出色，但不必全是精心剪辑的视频、旋转的信息图表、来回滑动的特效。（01:06:50）：这种形式并非传达信息的必要条件。因此，我们正在推出一个完整的项目和流程，通过它，你会看到我们发布更多视频，部分源于这个洞察，但更重要的是，我的团队有许多专家，他们有很多精彩内容要分享。所以我正努力让团队发挥作用，让他们明白杜阿尔特不等于南希·杜阿尔特。我们有许多专家在杜阿尔特工作，你看他们的任何视频，都能感受到杜阿尔特的方向。他们都是才华横溢的专家，世界级的专家。这就是我们的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you have a similar challenge to me where I named my newsletter, Lenny's Newsletter.
turns.zh: 我觉得你也面临着类似的挑战，我把我的新闻简报命名为《莱尼的笔记》。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, same thing.
turns.zh: 是啊，一样的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:07:33] talk about that.
turns.zh: [01:07:33]（音频不清晰）谈谈这个吧。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Same thing.
turns.zh: 一样的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, can never be anyone else. It's a challenge, but yeah, don't know, it worked out. Okay. Actually, real final question before we get to a very exciting lightning round. Have you seen examples of product managers specifically telling really good stories?
turns.zh: 是啊，我永远也成不了别人。虽然这很挑战，但说实话，最后还是成功了。好的。实际上，最后一个问题，然后我们就进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。你们有没有见过产品经理特别善于讲故事的例子？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: The product management process has multiple phase. There's the creative explorative process all the way through to getting it produced. And I think story can take you along in each phase. So, there's example, which I read about, I wasn't actually even part of, but Brian Chesky at Airbnb, there was a whole article where he unpacked this moment in their product development cycle where they decided they would take a walk in the shoes of their customer and they hired a Pixar illustrator to illustrate each scene as the team's like, okay, okay, they said this is her name. And they were like, okay, what happens? Her alarm goes off. Okay, what happens next? What happens next? Okay, now she's decided she needs to book something. What does she do? She wants to do that. They realized from this little walk in the shoes of their customer just this day in the life, which is a classic storytelling method for any product, they realized that they had their strategy wrong, that they needed to move as soon as possible to a mobile first strategy. (01:08:46): And it was just because they actually thought about, okay. She goes, brushes their teeth, they do this. They were just literally walking through the life of their ideal customer and that was when they realized they had it all messed up. But the other phases, after all this work people put into product and the making of the product and the managing of pushing it through. We have a large client that makes shoes or athletic things. I love telling stories, but I can't say this. And there's this moment where we get brought in and could you please train our product people in story? We're like, "What's the big problem?" They're like, "They'll spend a year or two on a shoe and be like, chunk, put it on the table. And they're like, what do you have to say about it?" They're like, "It's red." And it's like all these years of investment, all these years, they couldn't unpack any sort of story or any sort of reason or even their passion for why they chose red. (01:09:41): And it was like, here's my shoe, it's red. And so this ability to move things along by adding meaning or why and then wrapping it in a story actually can get a product chosen or rejected or there's just so many examples of different spaces in the product cycle that could benefit from a really well told story from, like I said, how the products innovate in the roadmap all the way through to what gets accepted. And then the big reveal, you think about even all the big Apple launches, it's about a big product reveal. It's about revealing this thing that had been hidden for so long and it's another moment to tell amazing stories. So, that's kind of a little bit of an insight on the product side of how to use story.
turns.zh: 产品管理流程有多个阶段。从创意探索阶段一直到产品落地阶段。我认为故事可以贯穿每个阶段。比如我读到的Airbnb的布莱恩·切斯基（Brian Chesky）的案例，虽然我没有亲身参与，但整篇文章详细描述了他们在产品开发周期中的一次关键决策——他们决定设身处地为客户着想，于是聘请了皮克斯的插画师为每个场景绘制草图。当团队成员描述“好的，好的，她叫这个名字。”然后“好的，接下来会发生什么？”“接下来会发生什么？”“好的，现在她决定预订房间。她要怎么做？”他们意识到，通过这种“一天生活”的体验式思考——这也是任何产品常用的经典故事讲述方法——他们发现战略方向有误，需要尽快转向移动优先策略。（01:08:46）这只是因为他们真正思考了客户的全过程：她起床、刷牙、做这些事……他们只是在真实地体验理想客户的生活，才意识到自己把一切都搞砸了。但在产品研发、制造和推广的其他阶段呢？我们有一个大型客户，生产鞋类或运动装备。我喜欢讲故事，但我不能透露细节。有一次，我们被请去培训他们的产品团队讲故事。我们问：“有什么大问题吗？”他们回答：“他们会花一两年时间设计一款鞋子，然后突然扔到桌上，问‘你们怎么想？’他们会说‘是红色的’。多年的投入，换来的却是一句‘是红色的’。”这就是用故事赋予意义、讲清缘由，甚至激发激情的力量——它能让产品被选中或淘汰。在产品周期中，从路线图中的创新到最终验收，每个阶段都有大量案例能从精彩的故事中获益。就连苹果的大型发布会，也是通过惊艳的故事来揭示长期保密的成果。这就是产品侧如何运用故事的深刻见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Airbnb example is an awesome example. It's all true. When I joined Airbnb is actually right there in the process of doing that.
turns.zh: Airbnb的例子太棒了。都是真实的。我加入Airbnb时，他们正处于这个阶段。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个例子了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they ended up drawing these key frames of the journey as you described, and they put it right in the center of the office. Here's the journey of a host and a guest that's like 12 frames of that journey. And that actually became the strategy of the company is let's pick six of these frames and make them awesome. And that's what we're going to do.
turns.zh: 他们最终把你描述的旅程关键帧画了出来，还把它挂在了办公室的正中央。这是房东和客人的旅程，共有12个关键帧。后来这成了公司的策略——选出六个关键帧并把它们做得尽善尽美。我们就要这么做。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Make booking experience awesome. Make the arrival experience awesome. So, there's a lot of truth to that.
turns.zh: 要让预订体验变得棒，要让抵达体验变得棒。确实很有道理。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: And it was visualized, right? The vision was visualized like what you're saying we're headed in the future. And it was super clear. I love that story. So cool you were there.
turns.zh: 这些画面被具象化了，对吧？那个愿景被具象化了，就像你说的，这就是我们未来的方向。非常清晰。我喜欢这个故事。你当时在场真是太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it was very cool. And they actually were very mobile. You could grab one of these drawings and bring it to your desk and how are we going to make this moment better this week?
turns.zh: 是啊，确实很酷。他们还非常灵活。你可以拿起其中一幅画，带到自己的办公桌前，讨论这周怎么能让这个时刻更美好。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it was actually indeed, Pixar storyboard artist that they hired for a year. That was his job. Draw these key frames.
turns.zh: 而且他们确实雇了皮克斯的故事板艺术家，为期一年。这就是他的工作。画这些关键帧。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Oh, that's amazing.
turns.zh: 哦，太惊人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it connects so directly with your point about empathy. That was the epitome of empathy. Here's what the guest and hosts are going through, and here's where we can do better.
turns.zh: 这和你的共情观点直接相关。这就是共情的典范。这就是客人和房东正在经历的，以及我们可以如何改进的地方。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah, it's amazing. Yeah, it does tie together.
turns.zh: 是啊，太惊人了。确实紧密相连。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If folks want to look this up, by the way, we'll link in the show notes. If you just Google Snow White Airbnb, you can watch a video of how they all kind of came about this. Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you if you're ready.
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，如果大家想查阅相关资料，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。只要在谷歌上搜索“白雪公主Airbnb”，就能观看整个过程的视频。好的，接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。如果你准备好了，我有六个问题要问你。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yep, I'm ready.
turns.zh: 好的，我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I think I always classically recommend the gospels because there's just so much love and groundbreaking thinking there. And then for people who do wind up taking an interest in story, I think one of the best books, if you want to pick that up, is Chris Vogler's, The Writer's Journey, where he took Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey, made it 12 Steps, and he was a Disney story analyst. So, it's just really classic body of work that had really helped people get their minds around story and the archetypes.
turns.zh: 我通常会推荐福音书，因为其中充满了爱和开创性的思想。对于那些对故事感兴趣的人来说，克里斯·沃格勒的《作家的旅程》是必读之作。他把约瑟夫·坎贝尔的“英雄之旅”分解成12个步骤，而他本身就是迪士尼的故事分析师。所以，这是一部非常经典的著作，帮助人们理解故事和原型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: It's my little sinful pleasure. It's way into K drama, Korean drama. Don't even ask me how, but I'm way into that. I've seen almost all of them now. I'm at the bottom of the barrel of them.
turns.zh: 这是我小小的罪恶乐趣。我沉迷于韩国电视剧。别问我怎么开始的，但我真的很着迷。现在我几乎看完了所有韩国电视剧，真是入了魔了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite?
turns.zh: 有最喜欢的吗？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: No, my husband just watched one. It's called Business Proposal, and he watched it with me and he's like, oh no, now I'm going to be hooked too. They're just real. They're just cute as a button. And they have a longer arc. They're like an epic length tail. They drop in 12 part seasons or one season 12. Anyway, don't even get me started. It sounds dumb, because I like the epic tales and the dramas, but they're cute.
turns.zh: 没有，我丈夫刚看了一部。叫《商业提案》，他和我一起看的，然后说天啊，我也要被它迷住了。他们太真实了。简直萌得让人心都要化了。而且剧情线更长。就像史诗级长篇幅的尾巴。分成12集一季，或者一季12集。反正别让我说下去了。这听起来有点傻，因为我喜欢宏大的叙事和剧情片，但他们就是太可爱了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我超爱这部剧。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: They're just cute.
turns.zh: 他们就是太萌了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. Getting very real. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask people that you're hiring?
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到正题，你面试新人时最喜欢问什么问题？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Oh, favorite interview question. We ask a lot about who they are. So, we use psychometrics a lot here, and we really understand who they are, and we actually ask people to tell a story. And if that's uncomfortable or those psychometrics are uncomfortable, they're not really a fit, because we are a systemic story culture, and we define empathy at the company as know yourself, accept yourself, kind of work on yourself, and then adapt to others. So, if people aren't open to really understanding how they show up then and then adapt and change under our care, then we don't hire them.
turns.zh: 哦，最喜欢的面试问题。我们会深入了解应聘者的性格。所以我们常用心理测评工具，通过让他们讲故事来了解他们的真实面目。如果他们对此感到不适，或者心理测评结果不理想，那他们就不太适合我们公司，因为我们奉行系统化叙事文化，公司的核心价值观是了解自己、接纳自己、不断成长，并适应他人。所以如果有人不愿意真正理解自己、在我们的指导下调整和改变，那我们就不会录用他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近发现的你特别喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: I'm excited about a tool I just paid for last week. It's called writer.com. So, it's built on multiple language models and including, it's going to be trained on our own, all my IP, all my books, every blog post, it'll learn the voice and it'll use my own kind of language model to help us write faster. So, we put really good prompts in and we get a really good product out. So, I'm super excited about that.
turns.zh: 我对上周刚付费购买的writer.com特别兴奋。这款工具基于多语言模型构建，还能根据我的知识产权进行深度训练，包括我的所有书籍、博客文章等，它能学习我的表达风格，利用专属语言模型帮助我们提高写作效率。只需输入优质的提示语，就能产出优质内容。我对此超级期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm actually an investor in that company, so this is great to hear.
turns.zh: 我恰好是这家公司的投资者，所以听到这个消息真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Writer.com. What is something relatively minor you've changed in your approach to developing presentations that has had a big impact on your ability to execute and get them out?
turns.zh: writer.com。开发演示文稿时，你在方法上做过哪些相对微小的改进，却对执行和产出效果产生了巨大影响？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's the biggest roadblock for so long that made things painful was the edit cycles. How do we do a round with a client? Then you have multiple version, then you have version control. So, we've come up with this annotation system, so everyone on a project knows exactly the status of that slide, and there's no way really to check slides in and out. And so we've come up with this amazing, beautiful, very visual process where everyone knows the exact status of the slide, and it's really easy. You could put it in thumbnail mode and be like, hmm, we're 80% complete. Everyone's going to focus on just these two things. So, that part of the process, especially enterprise at scale where 20 or 30 people are contributors to a deck. That process we made is the clients are really liking it.
turns.zh: 是的。长期以来最大的障碍是编辑周期。和客户沟通需求、多次版本迭代、版本控制等等。我们开发了一套注释系统，这样项目组每个人都能清晰了解幻灯片的进展状态，不需要频繁签入签出。通过这个直观的流程，每个人都能准确掌握幻灯片进度，一目了然。用户可以切换到缩略图模式，查看完成度达80%等关键信息，专注于最重要的两点。这个流程在大规模企业中特别实用，比如有20、30人参与制作的演示文稿项目。客户对此反响非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To leave people with one final tip to give better presentations. What would that be?
turns.zh: 最后给出一个提升演示效果的终极小技巧。是什么？

turns.speaker: Nancy Duarte
turns.en: To become a better presenter, pick a topic you are passionate about, something where you're like, oh my gosh, I've got to see this happen. And pick that topic and be so passionate about it. Work on that talk or stand up at a volunteer thing and really work on something that makes you feel passionate. And then in the future when you're presenting something that you're not passionate about, everything you learned will apply to a business presentation, but you're going to have that feeling. You're going to know what it's like to present from your soul and from a place of passion and the great presenters tap into that passion point and pull from that, and that's what makes them a great presenter on other topics, that they might not be as passionate about.
turns.zh: 想要成为更出色的演讲者，就要选择一个你真正热爱的话题——一个让你激动不已、迫切想亲眼见证其实现的主题。专注于这个话题，投入热情地准备演讲，或是在志愿活动中发言，真正从内而外激发你的热情。这样当你未来面对自己不感兴趣的演讲任务时，所学的技巧仍能应用于商业演示，但你会带着真情实感——你会知道如何从灵魂深处、从激情之源出发进行演讲。优秀的演讲者总能触及这种激情源泉，并从中汲取力量，这也正是他们在其他不那么感兴趣的主题上也能表现出色的原因。
